title: Evaluate Value, Risk, and Harm Together
editorial_note: Automated dialogue draft from the revised lesson. Review spoken wording and meaning before publishing.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Today we're talking about Evaluate Value, Risk, and Harm Together. By the end, you'll know why this matters, how to use it, and what to notice in a real product.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What is the problem we are trying to understand?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Product cases often quantify intended benefit and describe harm separately in a late review. Evaluate them together because the mechanism creating value may also create risk. Faster matching can reduce effort while increasing reliance on stale data. More verification can improve accuracy while excluding providers with lower capacity.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Personalisation can improve relevance while collecting sensitive data.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Value and harm are properties of the same system
turns.text: What changes when we look at value and harm are properties of the same system?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Map:

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: direct users, affected non-users, staff, partners, and communities; intended benefit and how it is produced; burden, lost option, or risk created by the same mechanism; who has power to choose, avoid, detect, contest, and recover; distribution across context and group; evidence, uncertainty, and time horizon.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Aggregate benefit cannot silently cancel concentrated harm, especially when those harmed have less choice or recourse.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at describe risk as a scenario?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: “Privacy risk” or “bias risk” is too abstract to design. Write:

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Because condition or mechanism, affected person may experience event and consequence, while detection/recovery condition makes it more or less severe.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Assess:

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: severity of consequence; likelihood or plausibility with uncertainty; exposure and duration; detectability before harm; reversibility and residual effect; ability and cost to obtain recourse; distribution and structural vulnerability; potential for repetition or amplification.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Avoid multiplying weak numeric estimates into false precision. Use bands with evidence and rationale. A rare catastrophic or rights-related harm may require a hard constraint even when expected-value arithmetic looks small.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at use a control hierarchy?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Prefer controls that reduce risk at its source:

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: 1. Avoid: do not create the capability or use case. 2. Reduce scope: limit population, data, authority, attribute, or consequence. 3. Change the system: remove hazardous defaults, repair data/policy, redesign workflow. 4. Prevent: validation, permissions, separation of duties, accessible interaction, safe thresholds. 5.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Detect and contain: monitoring, audit, anomaly detection, pause, suppression. 6. Recover and remedy: correction, fallback, appeal, support, compensation, communication. 7. Inform: explanation and warning where people can act.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Disclosure is a weak primary mitigation when the organisation can remove the hazard. Consent does not legitimise an unsafe or coercive arrangement. Human review is not protective without capacity, evidence, authority, and independence.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at include misuse, non-use, and externalities?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Ask how the system may be used beyond intent, including internal shortcut, coercive use, proxy decisions, data reuse, and optimisation pressure. Examine people who cannot or will not use it: does the alternate route deliver comparable quality or punish refusal?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Look beyond the transaction. Verification notifications consume attention; data infrastructure requires maintenance; provider ranking changes demand; staff absorb edge cases; environmental and vendor dependencies create longer-term costs. These externalities belong in the product decision.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Evaluate controls as real service capabilities
turns.text: What changes when we look at evaluate controls as real service capabilities?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Test controls under the condition that invokes them. Can a screen-reader user perceive conflict? Can support suppress a record at night? Does rollback correct every channel? Can a smaller clinic use the alternate route? Does an appeal change outcome? Monitor the control’s performance and unintended burden.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Risk is dynamic. Reassess when population, policy, data, model, source, channel, business incentive, or authority changes. A safe pilot boundary does not automatically remain safe at scale.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: lending pre-approval?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A fast pre-approval flow creates convenience and commercial value. It can also expose sensitive data, reproduce unequal historical access, appear more final than it is, or deny people without usable recourse.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Strong mitigation may require narrowing the use, separating education from decision, providing adverse-action explanation and correction, independent review, outcome monitoring, and refusing automation where the institution cannot carry the risk.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at where this can go wrong?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Benefit ledger only: intended value is quantified while burden and externality remain prose. Average-value cancellation: aggregate improvement hides concentrated severe harm. Risk nouns: “privacy” or “bias” appears without a scenario, mechanism, or affected person. Likelihood theatre: unsupported numbers make uncertain harm look managed.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Disclosure mitigation: warning transfers a preventable institutional risk to the user. Human-review fiction: oversight lacks capacity, evidence, authority, or independence. Checklist closure: naming a control is treated as evidence it works. Unowned residual risk: no legitimate role accepts, monitors, pauses, and remedies.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does the harder design decision appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Senior practitioners connect ethics to product mechanics and decision rights. They challenge who defines acceptable risk, whose evidence is missing, and whether people can realistically refuse or recover.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: They distinguish reversible experimentation from exposure that creates lasting harm and are prepared to recommend narrower scope or no build when the organisation lacks protective capability.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: <! -- Editorial: manual revision; curated product example --

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we see that in a concrete product situation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Illustrative scenario: a rent-payment product. Automatic payment may reduce missed deadlines while creating overdraft risk for people with irregular income. Evaluate benefit, business value, reversibility, notice, support burden, and unequal harm together. A high adoption rate is not a complete answer if a subgroup bears the cost of the design.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should I notice the next time I use a product?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Choose a product that handles health, money, identity, work, safety, or automated judgement. Find its main value promise, then ask which group could experience the opposite outcome. Is the protection prevention, detection, recovery, or merely disclosure? Try to locate the accountable appeal or remedy.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: If it ends at “contact support,” inspect whether support can actually change the decision.
